query: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa, but its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. What single intervention could improve its room-temperature compressive strength–plasticity balance without sacrificing its high strength? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, the operative mechanism, the predicted change in strength and plasticity relative to the equiatomic disordered-BCC alloy, the conditions and limits under which the effect should occur, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A targeted thermal treatment that induces nanometer‐scale Mo-rich (B2) precipitates within the continuous disordered BCC matrix of equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo will locally partition and reduce the high effective electronegativity difference in the load‐bearing matrix, thereby enhancing room‐temperature ductility while retaining high yield strength via precipitation strengthening.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic, as‐cast disordered-BCC NbZrTiHfMo with a homogeneous elemental distribution and high Mo content that yields ~1719 MPa compressive strength but limited plasticity.
generation.intervention: Perform a two-step heat treatment: first, a homogenization solutionizing step at an elevated temperature (e.g., ~1400°C for a short duration) to reset the microstructure, followed by an aging treatment at a moderate temperature (~600°C) for an extended period (e.g., ~120 hours) to induce the controlled formation of nanometer-scale, discontinuous Mo-rich B2 precipitates within the BCC matrix.
generation.conditions: This effect is expected to occur under ambient pressure with the aging treatment carefully tuned so that the B2 phase forms as fine, dispersed precipitates rather than a continuous network; the process window must avoid excessive coarsening (which would reduce strength) and insufficient aging (which would not improve plasticity). Room-temperature compressive testing conditions will assess the performance.
generation.structural_mediator: The size, distribution, and coherence of the induced Mo-rich B2 precipitates that alter the local chemical environment of the surrounding BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Partitioning of Mo into discrete B2 precipitates reduces the effective electronegativity difference in the contiguous disordered BCC matrix, facilitating easier dislocation motion (and thus enhanced plasticity) while the dispersed precipitates act as obstacles that maintain or even slightly improve the high yield strength via precipitation strengthening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the initial as-cast alloy, the heat-treated material will exhibit an improved compressive plastic strain (for example, ductility increasing from very low levels (<5%) to values on the order of >16% compressive strain) while retaining a compressive yield strength on the order of ~1700 MPa, thereby achieving a superior strength–plasticity balance.
generation.baseline: As-cast equiatomic disordered-BCC NbZrTiHfMo alloy with high yield strength (~1719 MPa) but limited ductility due to the uniformly high Mo-induced electronegativity difference.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold as long as the heat treatment produces a fine, discrete B2 precipitate dispersion without transforming the matrix into a continuous brittle phase; if the aging parameters are not within the optimal window, a coarser or continuous B2 phase may form, which could diminish ductility or even lower strength.
generation.uncertainty: While prior work (e.g., PMC5995863 on microstructure inversion in similar refractory HEAs and PMC7514121 on the role of Mo in elemental strengthening) supports that controlled phase separation can improve ductility through microstructural design, it remains uncertain how the optimal aging conditions and precipitate characteristics will translate specifically in NbZrTiHfMo. The precise control over precipitate size and distribution in a high-Mo system is not yet established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloy samples: one set as as-cast (control) and one set subjected to the two-step heat treatment (solutionizing at ~1400°C for a short, fixed time and aging at ~600°C for ~120 hours). Characterize the microstructures using TEM and XRD, confirming the formation of discrete Mo-rich B2 precipitates within the BCC matrix. Perform standardized room-temperature compressive tests on both sets.
measurements: TEM imaging and precipitate size/distribution statistics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the heat-treated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature compressive plasticity (e.g., no increase from <5% to >16% strain) while maintaining their yield strength within ±10% of the as-cast value, or if microstructural analysis reveals an undesired continuous or overly coarse B2 phase distribution, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The main goal of the present work was to improve the room temperature ductility of an initially brittle RHEA through microstructure modifications by thermal treatment. The goal was successfully achieved and an improved balance of high strength and good compressive ductility was demonstrated by “inverting” the microstructure from a continuous B2 matrix with discrete BCC precipitates to one consisting of a continuous BCC matrix with discrete B2 precipitates. The details of the strengthening mechanisms in these microstructures are beyond of the scope of the present study. However, it can be speculated that strong element bonding in the B2 matrix is responsible for high strength (and, unfortunately, brittleness) of Condition (1); while in the case of Conditions (2) and (3), precipitation strengthening from B2 precipitates and dislocation mobility in BCC matrix are likely to play a substantial role. Classical precipitation hardening models provide guidance on material parameters that must be quantified to predict the level of strengthening in the present alloys, and more recent models specifically address the influence of coherent B2 precipitates within a disordered BCC matrix in HEAs a

AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect
